title: Drugs in Philip K. Dick
note: Generated from findings.py, which is hand-curated. Edit findings.py and re-run build_inventory.py; do not edit this file by hand. Raw sweep output is regenerable with scripts/research/sweep_corpus.py --profile drugs.

evidence_packets.claim: Dick took amphetamines for roughly twenty years, from the early 1950s to 1972: first as prescribed Semoxydrine (methamphetamine), then in escalating and partly street-bought quantities. He gave two reasons, depression and the volume of writing his low advances demanded.
evidence_packets.summary: Letters of 1962–1976, the Platt interview (1979), Exegesis section 016, and the three biographies. The figures differ: 'about 18 years' (1976), 'twenty years' (Rickman), 'nearly twenty years' (Sutin).

evidence_packets.claim: Dick's psychedelic experience was small and mostly bad: LSD on two or three occasions from 1964, one large dose of mescaline in May 1970 that he credited with the love in Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said, and a 1968 dose of what turned out to be PCP. How many times, and when, the sources dispute.
evidence_packets.summary: Letters of 1965–1977, the Vertex (1974) and Platt (1979) interviews, Sutin, Anne R. Dick and Rickman.

evidence_packets.claim: Dick repeatedly said The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch (written 1964) was written before he had taken LSD, from reading; Harlan Ellison printed in 1967 that it was LSD-inspired, apparently with Dick's encouragement.
evidence_packets.summary: Letters of 1967 and 1969, the Vertex and Platt interviews, Sutin and Anne R. Dick. They disagree on the source of the novel's drugs: an article by Aldous Huxley, or reading about hallucinogenic mushrooms.

evidence_packets.claim: After Nancy Hackett left in 1970, Dick's Santa Venetia house became a crash-pad for young users and his amphetamine use peaked: by his own report to a psychiatrist in 1971, a thousand Methedrine tablets a week.
evidence_packets.summary: Letters of 1970, VALIS (fiction), Sutin, Anne R. Dick's interviews with the house's residents, and Arnold.

evidence_packets.claim: After a suicide attempt in Vancouver in March 1972 Dick spent some weeks at X-Kalay, a Synanon-style rehabilitation house for heroin addicts, and came out an evangelist against drugs. By 1975 he thought its lessons faulty, and later compared its 'game' to brainwashing.
evidence_packets.summary: Letters of 1972–1975, Exegesis 1976–79, the Vertex interview, Sutin.

evidence_packets.claim: A Scanner Darkly (written 1973, published 1977) is Dick's account of the 1970–72 drug culture: its characters are based on people he knew, its Author's Note lists the dead and damaged, and it puts Dick himself on the list. He later read it as being about something other than drugs.
evidence_packets.summary: The novel and its Author's Note; letters of 1973–1977; the Rickman interview (1981); the Exegesis, 1976–80.

evidence_packets.claim: Dick's fictional drugs are almost all traps: Can-D and Chew-Z, JJ-180, Substance D. Each one is addictive, each one is owned by someone, and in each the user's reality becomes another's.
evidence_packets.summary: Now Wait for Last Year, A Scanner Darkly and VALIS in this archive; The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch through Dick's comments and criticism (the novel's text is not in the corpus).

evidence_packets.claim: Dick named chemical factors in the experiences of February–March 1974 — sodium pentothal from oral surgery, a large dose of water-soluble vitamins, lithium — but held that they disinhibited something rather than produced it.

In the Exegesis Dick turned intoxication into theology: John Allegro's sacred mushroom, Hofmann on LSD at Eleusis, Dionysos; mankind 'drugged + intoxicated' in a false world; Substance D as a picture of the human condition. He also says 2-3-74 was not a drug experience.

The biographers disagree on how much and when: Anne R. Dick's Point Reyes years against Arnold's 'massive doses'; Sutin's two LSD trips against Anne R. Dick's one; Arnold's amphetamine psychosis against Rickman's 'imagination'; Sutin's sobriety after 1972 against Arnold's 'some assert'.
evidence_packets.summary: Sutin (1989), Rickman (1984), Anne R. Dick (1995/2010), Arnold (2016). Anthony Peake's biography is catalogued but its text is not in this archive.

evidence.anchor: I stumbled on a stimulant drug called semoxydrene
evidence.editorial_note: Semoxydrine was a brand of methamphetamine hydrochloride (Dick learns this himself in October 1964: DRG-LET-1964-BROCHURE).

card.context: A long autobiographical letter about agoraphobia. Dick says that at twenty-four — around 1952–53 — two things pulled him out of a closing-in world: teaching himself to drive, and a stimulant he spells semoxydrene. The first 5 mg, he writes, gave back the clarity he had been losing for fifteen years and let him see the delusion he had been living in. Later in the letter the "little green pills" save him and then deliver him to a disastrous move. The earliest dated account of his amphetamine use in the archive, and it is an account of a cure.
card.pith: the first 5 mg which I took cleared away the cobwebs from my brain
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: my supply of amphetamines has dried up

card.context: A comic letter from Oakland, months after leaving Anne and the Point Reyes house. In among the cats and the Avon Lady, Dick complains that his amphetamines have run out despite two open prescriptions, and jokes about something injectable instead. The tone is play; the fact underneath is that by 1964 he was managing a supply.
card.pith: I don’t even know why my supply of amphetamines has dried up, and I had two open prescriptions.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Terry and Carol Carr, October 22, 1964

evidence.anchor: I am up to six 7.5 mg of them a day

card.context: Dick reports to the Carrs that a druggist forgot to remove the brochure from his refill, so after seven years ("or is it nine?") he has finally read what his pills are: semoxydrine hydrochloride is methamphetamine. He is up to the strongest dose, six a day, and quotes the warning that overdose can cause hallucinations and death with mock horror. Sutin reprints the passage as the epigraph to his account of these years.
card.pith: I am up to six 7.5 mg of them a day, and 7.5 is their strongest dose
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: how does the LSD experience resemble an actual, authentic psychotic interlude

card.context: Written for a fanzine discussion. Dick compares an eight-hour psychotic episode of a few weeks earlier — triggered, he thinks, by deaths and money troubles — with the LSD experience: the same amplified senses, the same lost time sense, a delusion that an outside force was directing him. He then proposes that the LSD trip resembles the Bardo Thodol, and recalls that his first trip put him in Rome during the Punic Wars, speaking Latin.
card.pith: when I took LSD the first time I believed myself back in Rome, during the Punic Wars
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: The second time (under LSD) I perceived Him
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Dick describes two encounters with an evil, judging deity. The first, a face in the sky with empty-slot eyes, he "subsequently wrote ... up" in The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, "which is a 'trip' book". The second came under LSD, a vengeful presence demanding an audit, which he answered with the Latin of the Requiem. A 1967 statement that ties the novel to a vision and the vision to the drug vocabulary, without quite saying the novel came from LSD.
card.pith: The second time (under LSD) I perceived Him as a pulsing, furious, throbbing mass of vengeance
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: My first LSD experience, by the way, confirmed
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch
evidence.editorial_note: The letter carries no catalogue date; the dateline in its body reads June 8, 1969.

card.context: Answering a critic's questions, Dick says the face of Palmer Eldritch, with its slotted eyes, was something he saw objectively over the landscape — "a true trip, before I had seen any LSD, much less taken any" — and that he joined the Anglo-Catholic Church to protect himself from it. His first LSD experience, he adds, confirmed the vision: a hell-world it took two thousand subjective years to crawl out of.
card.pith: My first LSD experience, by the way, confirmed my vision of Palmer Eldritch
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: With acid I never had any genuine insights

card.context: Dick announces that he has finished Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said, "a novel which truly satisfies me", and that it is an affirmation rather than another question about what is real. It is based in part, he says, on one large dose of mescaline, which gave him what acid never had: an overpowering love for other people, which he put into the novel. The same letter mentions rereading his old novels after "a great number of amphetamines".
card.pith: With acid I never had any genuine insights, but on the mescalin I was overwhelmed by terribly powerful feelings
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Mr. and Mrs. White, November 24, 1970

evidence.anchor: I took one thousand methamphetamine tablets in two weeks

card.context: A long letter from the Santa Venetia house, among friends who have talked each other out of suicide. Dick offers his resilience as proof: he took a thousand methamphetamine tablets in two weeks, crashed, and forty-eight hours later was on the phone and driving to buy a new stylus. Earlier in the same letter he wonders whether his happiness is the speed, and decides it is not.
card.pith: I took one thousand methamphetamine tablets in two weeks, then crashed
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: By and large, X-Kalay works with heroin addicts
evidence.editorial_note: Catalogued as undated; the dateline in the body reads April 3, 1972.

card.context: Written from inside X-Kalay. Dick tells a Swedish correspondent that after a collapse in Vancouver he tried to kill himself, that Suicide Prevention sent him to the X-Kalay Foundation, and that its regime — constant company, hard physical work, isolation from everything he knew — is rebuilding him. The house works mainly with heroin addicts out of Canadian prisons, and he is living among them.
card.pith: I owe my life to them.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: X-Kalay turned out to be by-and-large a heroin rehabilitation organization
evidence.editorial_note: Catalogued as undated; the dateline in the body reads October 31, 1972.

card.context: Six months later, from Fullerton, Dick gives Gillespie the story of Vancouver: the suicide attempt, a month at X-Kalay, the attack therapy that pulled him out of depression within a week. The centre of the letter is what he saw there: heroin addicts with insect eyes who calculate what you are worth, a girl addicted at fourteen, a woman of twenty-four taken for fifty. His "murderous hate toward drug dealers", he says, comes from them.
card.pith: No reduction of the human into a mere thing, short of removing actual sections of the brain, can be found outside of the dismal transformation brought on by heroin addiction.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: the misuse of drugs, dangerous and illegal drugs

card.context: Explaining the Vancouver suicide attempt, Dick puts it down to the depression that followed losing his wife and child — and then names drugs as a cause of that loss: marijuana, hashish and, worst, LSD had helped put his wife in a mental hospital twice. He now sees these drugs as a major cause of everything that brought him to the attempt. His own amphetamines are not on the list.
card.pith: I saw these drugs as a major cause of the problems that had brought me to attempt suicide.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to Nina and Jim, January 6, 1973

evidence.anchor: five friends kill themselves during or as a result of acid trips

card.context: To friends at X-Kalay, Dick describes a live radio interview in Los Angeles where he said that X-Kalay meant more to him than science fiction, and that five friends had killed themselves during or after acid trips. The station, which was pro-drug, asked him to retract on air that good acid was fine. He refused.
card.pith: what I then said was that no acid was good.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: What influence would you say that LSD has had on your writing

card.context: Dick tells his daughter about the interview Vertex has just recorded. The interviewer's first question was what influence LSD had had on his writing; Dick answered "none at all", and the interviewer said plaintively that the whole first half of his piece was supposed to be about it. Dick tells it as a joke at the magazine's expense.
card.pith: and my answer was, “none at all.”
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: it was taking street dope, LSD probably

card.context: Dick has just finished the last page of A Scanner Darkly, after two years in which he could not write. A letter from his ex-wife arrives the same week: Nancy writes that street drugs, LSD probably, caused all three of her long psychotic episodes. He had guessed, he says, and notes the irony given the subject of the novel.
card.pith: Nancy says, for the first time, that it was taking street dope, LSD probably, that caused all three of her long psychotic episodes
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: It is a very anti-dope book
evidence.editorial_note: The dateline in the body reads "August 31 (if there is one), 1973". The research framing is a joke the letter itself undercuts; compare the Author's Note (DRG-NOTE-SCANNER-NOVEL).

card.context: To the Vancouver radio interviewer who had covered X-Kalay, Dick describes the novel he has finished: very anti-drug, about Substance D, which the heads call Slow Death because it burns out the brain until you cannot mop floors. He presents his years in the drug subculture, with a straight face that keeps slipping, as research for it — "(ask me how well I mop floors)".
card.pith: I even had to (ugh) partake of dope to get the true sense of it
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: in which I studied the drug-damaged brain

card.context: Dick explains to an English editor how 1974 began. He had been reading Robert Ornstein on the right hemisphere and the orthomolecular vitamin formula said to improve neural firing; he had just drafted A Scanner Darkly, where he concluded that the burned-out members of the drug subculture suffered from some split-brain impairment. Putting these together, he set out to switch on his own right hemisphere — and in mid-March got "abrupt, dazzling results".
card.pith: in which I studied the drug-damaged brain
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I did it mainly by ortho molecular formula vitamins

card.context: Dick writes to the psychologist whose work on hemispheric specialisation he had been reading, to ask what has become of him. Ten months ago, he says, he brought on his right hemisphere, mainly with the orthomolecular vitamins and concentrated meditation, and has been a different person since. The letter is also filed in the Exegesis.
card.pith: for ten months I have been a different person
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: the acid trip in 1964 was the head trip
evidence.editorial_note: The same letter is filed in the Exegesis (SEG_EXEG_1975-02-27_Claudia_01).

card.context: In the long letter on the death of his cat Pinky, Dick distinguishes what he saw in 1974 — a light that told him death had come and was real — from a drug experience. The 1974 events were not "a mere head trip"; the acid trip of 1964 was. It is one of the few places Dick dates his LSD use himself.
card.pith: I know the difference; the acid trip in 1964 was the head trip.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: this is obviously a mescaline type of experience
evidence.editorial_note: "Loaded" is ambiguous: the letter does not say on what. The Exegesis copy is SEG_EXEG_1975-02-27_Claudia_03.

card.context: Later in the same letter Dick describes a recent vision — vines swirling up the vestment of his saint statue, spring bursting out of winter — and compares it to a children's book he read long ago. He concedes it is "a mescaline type of experience", and that he was "loaded", then turns the concession: the author of the children's book had no mescaline, and the reproach that he saw it because he wanted to proves nothing.
card.pith: Now, this is obviously a mescaline type of experience. We know that. And I was loaded.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: the education which I got at X-Kalay

card.context: Left alone for a week while his wife and son were away, Dick found himself back in the conditions of Marin County after Nancy left — no money, no car, no friends — and this time liked it. He now thinks X-Kalay's education was faulty: it taught him that the individual alone is doomed, and left him dependent on others to survive. The lessons "burst into fragments".
card.pith: the education which I got at X-Kalay (the heroin rehab place in Vancouver) was faulty
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: it deals with people dying from street drugs

card.context: To a French translator, Dick calls A Scanner Darkly the best novel he has written and compares it to All Quiet on the Western Front: people dying from street drugs in a kind of war, where the protagonist at last falls alone and unnoticed. The dedication, he says, is a roll call of his dead and injured friends.
card.pith: The dedication to it is a rollcall of my dead and injured friends
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: wrote the story while on an LSD trip, which was not true
evidence.editorial_note: Oui's date for his first LSD — the early fifties — is contradicted by every other source, Dick's included.

card.context: A letter about marketing. Dick quotes Oui magazine's claim that he "started experimenting with LSD in the early fifties" and is an authority on pharmacology, and Paul Williams's Rolling Stone profile that "stressed the drug angle", as selling points for an editor. In the same breath he complains that Harlan Ellison told the world he wrote "Faith of Our Fathers" on an LSD trip.
card.pith: I not only was on drugs, but wrote the story while on an LSD trip, which was not true
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I have taken amphetamines, LSD, mescaline and phenothiazines

card.context: A numbered reply to a student's questionnaire, and the most compact account Dick ever gave. He has taken amphetamines, LSD, mescaline and phenothiazines; used amphetamines for about eighteen years, prescribed for depression, for energy because he was paid so little per book; took LSD only twice; no drug trip inspired anything except a passage in A Maze of Death. He takes no drugs now, and does not recommend them.
card.pith: I used amphetamines for about 18 years. They were prescribed for me due to depression.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: No drug trip has ever inspired me

card.context: The fourth answer in the same questionnaire. Asked whether drugs inspired his work, Dick names one exception: a small passage in A Maze of Death based on his first LSD experience. Sutin identifies it as the frozen landscape of snow and boulders in the novel's eleventh chapter, which Dick in 1974 called his LSD vision of 1964 "depicted with exact accuracy".
card.pith: No drug trip has ever inspired me to write anything except a small passage in my novel A MAZE OF DEATH
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: still under the influence of sodium pentathol
evidence.editorial_note: Dick spells it "pentathol" throughout; the drug is sodium pentothal (thiopental). The letter is also filed in the Exegesis.

card.context: Dick explains to his mother how many factors went into what he found in 1974. He had just had several teeth removed and was still under sodium pentothal; he was experimenting with the orthomolecular vitamin formula and had accidentally taken seven grams of vitamin C; and a girl came to the door wearing a gold fish necklace. The list is offered as explanation, not debunking.
card.pith: I was experimenting with the orthomolecular vitamin formula, and had accidentally taken 7 grams of vitamin C, much more than is indicated.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: All the characters are based on real dopers I knew

card.context: Thanking a fan for a Grateful Dead tape — his own reel-to-reel was stolen by junkies — Dick sends money for a copy of A Scanner Darkly. The book is set in Orange County, but the events are actual and happened in Marin; every character is a real doper he knew, most now dead or burned out, and Donna is as close as he could make her to a girl he loved.
card.pith: All the characters are based on real dopers I knew, most of whom are dead or burned out now
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: studied up on the orthomolecular vitamin formula

card.context: To the author of The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind, Dick explains that the experience behind his two most recent novels happened at the vernal equinox of 1974, after he had studied Ornstein and Bogen and begun the orthomolecular vitamins on purpose, to bring his right hemisphere into parity with the left.
card.pith: which is said to improve neural firing both in terms of synchronization and rate of fire
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: So Phil takes a hit of STP (DOM)
evidence.editorial_note: A plan for fiction, written in a letter: the "Phil" here is a character.

card.context: An outline for the novel that became VALIS, sent to his Bantam editor. A character called Phil, envious of friends who have met the entity Zebra, takes a hit of STP hoping to see it — and does. The outline then has Phil reflect that anything he saw would be put down to the drug, as Paige is called a nut and Nicholas a liar. In the published VALIS no one takes a psychedelic to meet the god.
card.pith: if Phil had come up with anything—in his case it would be attributed to psychedelic drugs
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Letter to James R. Bass, November 10, 1977

evidence.anchor: The first time I took LSD I saw the whole landscape freeze over

card.context: A letter of comfort to a depressed reader. Dick describes depression as an extended now in which time stops, like an LSD trip, and recalls his first trip as a frozen landscape of snow and rocks that lasted thousands of years. Hell, he has always believed, is cold.
card.pith: The first time I took LSD I saw the whole landscape freeze over
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: It starts with the suicide of a lovely gentle intelligent cultured young woman

card.context: Dick describes the autobiographical novel he has just sold to Bantam, in which he is three people. It begins where A Scanner Darkly ends, around 1971, with the LSD-caused suicide of a young woman, whose pointless death throws Horselover Fat into what looks like psychosis.
card.pith: It starts with the suicide of a lovely gentle intelligent cultured young woman, due to LSD
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: Nor was I any longer under the influence of the sodium pentathol

card.context: Dick tells the critic Patricia Warrick that when the world of the first century pushed through into his own in 1974, the causes he had listed elsewhere were absent: he held no convictions on the matter, the girl with the fish sign was gone, and he was no longer under the pentothal. The antique world came, he thinks, from a system of inner memories surfacing.
card.pith: Nor was I any longer under the influence of the sodium pentathol.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: what you can learn about yourself under the influence of sodium pentothal

card.context: Six months later, to the same correspondent, the pentothal is back in the story. The revelation of the fish sign happened while he was oblivious to his own nature, and it is amazing, he writes, what you can learn about yourself under sodium pentothal — he had been given a great deal for a wisdom-tooth extraction that day. He found he agreed with his unconscious completely.
card.pith: I guess I got in touch with my unconscious
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I have known a junky

card.context: Listing the kinds of people he has known — a bishop, a judge — Dick says the junky was the most humane of them. The man killed himself when his girlfriend was arrested; Dick once watched him give away his most treasured possession, a leather jacket Dick had bought him while he was withdrawing.
card.pith: the junky was the most humane
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I believe that the sodium pentathol and sight of the girl

card.context: Dick states the sceptical explanation himself — that the pentothal and the fish necklace threw a suggestible man into a hypnoidal state and he imagined everything — and asks how he then came to think in correct Greek. His answer keeps the drug as a cause: the pentothal and the girl were necessary, but what they did was release him from the contemporary world and make him remember.
card.pith: I believe that the sodium pentathol and sight of the girl wearing the fish necklace were necessary causal agents
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: the orthomolecular vitamins, esp. the overdose

card.context: "As to the events which preceded my experience": the vitamins, and above all the overdose of vitamin C, were crucial in synchronising neural firing, perhaps by flushing a built-up toxin. Then the thought that sodium pentothal is the "truth drug" — it de-hypnotised him, and the world of the Bible came back. The entry moves from pharmacology to the claim that it is still biblical times.
card.pith: the overdose (7 grams a day) of C is crucial, in regards to improving and synchronizing neural firing
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: There was some ancient equivilent, perhaps even drug induced

card.context: Dick suggests that the pentothal stood in for the trance of the ancient mysteries: an altered state known to early Christianity, perhaps itself drug-induced. What matters to him is that something outside and before the divine seizure caused his memory to return, if only for a second.
card.pith: There was some ancient equivilent, perhaps even drug induced.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: John Allegro was partially correct
evidence.editorial_note: Dated by the entry's own count, "30 months" after 2-3-74.

card.context: Reading the Eucharist's "do this in remembrance of me" as anamnesis — the early Christians finding themselves back at the time of the Saviour, as he did — Dick concludes that John Allegro, whose The Sacred Mushroom and the Cross derived Christianity from a mushroom cult, was partly right: the experience resembles psychedelics, in the good sense of doorways.
card.pith: This means that John Allegro was partially correct
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: perhaps my psychedelic experience paved the way

card.context: Later in the same entry: the unused neural circuits Bogen and Ornstein describe exist, and in him they fired. Something unknown is needed to cause the anamnesis — and his earlier psychedelic experience may have prepared the ground, as Castaneda's did. The drugs are allowed a role as preparation, not as cause.
card.pith: perhaps my psychedelic experience paved the way for me, a la Castaneda
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: a metabolic "toxin," mescalin-like, was secreted in my brain

card.context: Reviewing 1974 in clinical terms, Dick allows that it looks psychotic, but notes that he has been free of paranoid feelings for three whole years. His model: a mescaline-like metabolic toxin secreted in his own brain destroyed the persecutory complex. The psychedelic is now endogenous — a drug his body made.
card.pith: a metabolic "toxin," mescalin-like, was secreted in my brain
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: it is in fact not a study of hallucination + drugs
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Dick proposes that what the entity Zebra is doing can be inferred from The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch with its values reversed — and reports that on rereading, the novel turns out not to be about hallucination and drugs at all but about transubstantiation. Chew-Z is a eucharist.
card.pith: it is in fact not a study of hallucination + drugs but of the miracle of transubstantiation
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: to assume that substance D was secretly being produced by the government

card.context: Talking with K. W. Jeter about A Scanner Darkly's reception, Dick notes that readers, reviewers and the publishers all assume Substance D is secretly made by the government, to turn people into slave labour and for profit. The two agree that this can properly be inferred from the book — a reading Dick says he had not consciously put there.
card.pith: substance D was secretly being produced by the government
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: when I wrote the author's note to "Scanner" I meant

card.context: Dick reads his own Author's Note against the grain. When he wrote that its people were "punished entirely too much" he meant the drug's effects; read at the end of the novel, it seems instead to mean the lifetime in the New-Path work camp. The rehabilitation centre — modelled on X-Kalay — becomes the punishment.
card.pith: it more seems to refer to the lifetime incarceration at the new path work camp
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: is the exact analog of CP brainwashing

card.context: Working through A Scanner Darkly's last revelation — that the makers of Substance D want slaves, not money — Dick calls addiction and rehabilitation an establishment plot to recruit slave labour, and the Synanon game, the attack therapy he had undergone at X-Kalay, the exact equivalent of Communist brainwashing.
card.pith: The "Synanon game" is the exact analog of CP brainwashing
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: is a study of the punishment (too great) for playing instead of toiling
evidence.editorial_note: "After 4 years of exegesis re 'Tears'": the Tears exegesis begins in 1974.

card.context: Dick decides that A Scanner Darkly carries on the hidden theme of Flow My Tears: it does not deplore playing, only that way of playing. It is a study of the punishment — too great — for playing instead of toiling. "Not drugs." He is amazed that he wrote it before he had worked out Tears.
card.pith: is a study of the punishment (too great) for playing instead of toiling, not drugs
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: In LSD states you experience (1) apart from (2)

card.context: A model of three kinds of time: (1) inner time, (2) the outer world's time, (3) eternity. LSD separates (1) from (2), Dick argues, but never reaches (3); perhaps some psychedelic such as Amanita muscaria could. He himself reached (3) only in 2-3-74. The drug experience is placed one rung below the revelation.
card.pith: But never did I get to (3) except in 2-3-74.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I was intoxicated, not by LSD

card.context: After citing Hofmann's theory that LSD was used in the Greater Mysteries and Allegro's mushroom theory of early Christianity, Dick says that in 1974 he was indeed intoxicated — not by LSD, and not by a flashback, but by Valis. Then the reversal: ecstasy is sanity, sobriety is madness, and the secret was stolen for us by Dionysos. Behind Flow My Tears, he adds, lies the Bacchae.
card.pith: I was intoxicated, not by LSD - it wasn't a flash-back
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: John allegro was getting close to the truth
evidence.editorial_note: "As" may mean "as if" or "because"; the sentence does not settle whether he is claiming to have taken a mushroom. Spelling as in the manuscript.

card.context: The two things he is "not supposed to tell": the female nature of Christ, and that he is one of the early apostolic Christians. Allegro's The Sacred Mushroom and the Cross was close to the truth; Christianity is a shamanic religion in which another order of reality is experienced, and he crossed into it "as I had taken a pscyhedelic".
card.pith: I did pass over into "the other" world, all right, asd I had taken a pscyhedelic: (mushroom).
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: the other ingredient is: the sacred mushroom

card.context: The plasmate is Christ's blood: alive, information, drunk at the agape feasts. But it needs a second ingredient, the sacred mushroom, as a catalyst. Then, plainly: the drugs he took reacted with the plasmate in him, and it came alive. Here, unlike elsewhere, his own drug use is part of the mechanism.
card.pith: Well, the drugs I took reacted to the plasmate in me.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I must have gone mad (to be precise about it)
evidence.editorial_note: The entry refers to the Platt interview, which took place on 17 May 1979.

card.context: Dick inverts the usual story of 1974: he was not driven mad then but sobered up. He dates his madness to the 1950s or 1960s, "perhaps due to the speed", then to Nancy's psychosis around 1969; he was psychotic when he wrote Flow My Tears in 1970, and in 1971 and 1973; in early 1974 his psychotic "speed"-self collapsed and a sane self took over.
card.pith: I must have gone mad (to be precise about it) sometime back in the 50s or 60s, perhaps due to the speed
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I had been moving faster + faster for decades due to the amphetamines

card.context: In a theory of 2-3-74 as a timing failure, the amphetamines supply the mechanism: decades on them had speeded him up; without them his body made up the missing noradrenaline and he went faster still, until only timeless constants were visible. The withdrawal, not the drug, sets the stage.
card.pith: I had been moving faster + faster for decades due to the amphetamines.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: Driven mad by 1) Nancy leaving

card.context: Dick describes a fugal personality that "took over in 1970 when I took the mescalin", always high, intoxicated by amphetamines and cycling up and down with no relation to reality. Then he gives three causes for his madness, in order: Nancy leaving, drugs, endogenous psychosis. The drugs are one cause among three.
card.pith: Driven mad by 1) Nancy leaving; + 2) drugs; + 3) endogenous psychosis.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I'm no longer abusing drugs, legal or illegal

card.context: A stocktaking in the middle of the Exegesis: he has written his best book, his mind is alive, his daughters have visited, he is economically secure, he has been to France — and he is no longer abusing drugs, legal or illegal. "I am very happy." The next sentence wonders whether he has been dead since 1974.
card.pith: I'm no longer abusing drugs, legal or illegal - i.e. drug-dependent.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: Jeter says, "the fucked-up dopers

card.context: A dream of a cereal box printed like medicine directions convinces Dick that A Scanner Darkly holds the key: we are toxic, and the entity Zebra is a doctor chasing the poison — perhaps flushed out by his vitamins. Substance D's effects resemble tertiary syphilis; it was Hal Barris who showed the impaired brilliance the novel depicts. Then K. W. Jeter's remark, and Dick's turn to Dionysos, the mad god: are the sane really the insane?
card.pith: the fucked-up dopers -on Substance D- were the only ones who correctly understood the reality situation
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: no epistemological insight in my writing outweighs the study of brain impairment

card.context: If Christ is a physician using an advanced medical technology, Dick reasons, then nothing in his writing about knowledge and illusion outweighs A Scanner Darkly's study of brain damage from Substance D — which was based, he adds, on observation and experience of real impairment. The novel's double self is secondary to the damage.
card.pith: no epistemological insight in my writing outweighs the study of brain impairment
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: In SCANNER the cause of our being unable to reality-test
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Dick lays his novels side by side as one account. Tears shows the actual world, Rome around AD 45; Scanner shows why we cannot test reality — a damage to perception deliberately induced by a drug; and that matches the magician of Palmer Eldritch who drugs people into a world where no time passes. The fictional drugs become a diagnosis.
card.pith: an inner occlusion deliberately induced by a drug or drug-like substance
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: Hal was convinced that if sodium pentathol was given to me I'd remember

card.context: In the political version of 2-3-74, Hal Barris had predicted that under sodium pentothal Dick would remember a dissociated self — and he did: "Thomas". The pentothal was unexpected and let him wake up. A few lines on, the occluding force is thrown off "partly to the lithium + The vitamins, + of course the penta thil".
card.pith: Hal was convinced that if sodium pentathol was given to me I'd remember
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: Flushing (done by me with lithium

card.context: A numbered list of the conditions that set off his waking in 1974: sensory deprivation, intense fear, physical pain, a disinhibiting stimulus, the sodium pentothal, recognition of memories, closeness to death — and the flushing of his neural tissue with lithium and water-soluble vitamins in huge doses. Chemistry is two items in a list of nine.
card.pith: Flushing (done by me with lithium + ws vitaming in huge doses) of neural tissue.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: “The Acid Truth”, interview by Arthur Byron Cover, Vertex, February 1974 (in The Last Interview and Other Conversations)

evidence.anchor: All I ever found out about acid was that I was where I wanted to get out of fast

card.context: Asked whether "Faith of Our Fathers" was written on acid, Dick says you cannot write on acid — the one page he managed was in Latin. How much did he take? "Not that much." He is amazed by the blurbs he wrote for himself about experimenting with hallucinogens to find the reality beneath delusion.
card.pith: All I ever found out about acid was that I was where I wanted to get out of fast.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Interview by Arthur Byron Cover, Vertex, February 1974 (in PKD Magazine Interviews)

evidence.anchor: I wrote that before I had ever seen LSD
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: The fuller text of the Vertex interview. Dick knows of no effect LSD had on his work: Palmer Eldritch, "a tremendous bad acid trip, so to speak", was written before he had seen LSD, from a description of its discovery. Its drugs produced flashbacks before anyone knew LSD would — "an accidental prophecy".
card.pith: I wrote that before I had ever seen LSD.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Philip Purser, “Even Sheep Can Upset Scientific Detachment”, Daily Telegraph Magazine, July 19, 1974 (in PKD Magazine Interviews)

evidence.anchor: experimented with LSD but always under control

card.context: To an English journalist, Dick describes the vision of an evil, slot-eyed deity in the sky — the face he elsewhere calls Palmer Eldritch — seen from a rented shack in empty pastures where isolation worked like sensory deprivation: "I wasn't on LSD or any other drug, not at the time". Here he says its scanning gave him the title A Scanner Darkly. An evil form-destroyer strikes people alone, which is why LSD is so deadly. Purser adds that Dick had had "a bad time from drugs" and now does rehabilitation work.
card.pith: I’ve experimented with LSD but always under control.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Interview by Joe Vitale, The Aquarian, October 11–18, 1978 (in PKD Magazine Interviews)

evidence.anchor: Drugs cause the mind to feed on itself
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Asked whether drugs helped him see past illusion, Dick says absolutely not: drugs eat your head. He once thought enough psychedelics might show ultimate reality; now he thinks they show the patterns on the rug turning hideous, and lead to the rubber room. His drug experiences have not appeared in his work; Palmer Eldritch came from a Huxley article.
card.pith: There was a time in my life when I thought drugs could be useful
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: “Killing the Rat”, interview by Charles Platt, May 17, 1979 (in The Last Interview and Other Conversations)

evidence.anchor: The only drugs I took regularly were amphetamines

card.context: Charles Platt asks how far he was into drugs. The only drugs he took regularly, Dick says, were amphetamines, because he was paid so little per book: sixteen novels in five years, sixty finished pages a day. They were prescribed. He stopped, and does not write as much any more.
card.pith: the only way I could write that much was to take amphetamines, which were prescribed for me
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: “Killing the Rat”, interview by Charles Platt, May 17, 1979 (in The Last Interview and Other Conversations)

evidence.anchor: I used to talk like I was really into acid
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: The fullest account of his LSD use. He took it twice; the second dose may not have been acid at all. The first was Sandoz acid from the university, split with a friend, and he "went straight to hell". A month later the galleys of Palmer Eldritch arrived and he could not read them. "That was in 1964." He begged people not to take it.
card.pith: the fact of the matter is that I took it two times
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: “Killing the Rat”, interview by Charles Platt, May 17, 1979 (in The Last Interview and Other Conversations)

evidence.anchor: all I had had to go on when I wrote it was an article by Aldous Huxley
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: In the same answer: Palmer Eldritch is "my classic 'LSD novel'", written with nothing to go on but an Aldous Huxley article — and then everything horrible he had written seemed to come true under acid. The novel came first; the drug confirmed it.
card.pith: even though all I had had to go on when I wrote it was an article by Aldous Huxley
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: Interview by Gregg Rickman, September 30, 1981, in Philip K. Dick: In His Own Words (1984)

evidence.anchor: I wrote that to record them

card.context: Rickman asks about A Scanner Darkly, his first book to draw on the early 1970s. Dick dates his time in the drug subculture: after Nancy left in 1970, through 1971, and the first month of 1972. He began writing about those people a week after he left, to record them before they faded — and as an attack on drugs.
card.pith: And also as an attack on drugs because I had seen it kill so many people
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

source.citation: “Destruction and Enlightenment”, interview by Gregg Rickman, April 1981–February 1982 (in The Last Interview and Other Conversations)

evidence.anchor: score some marijuana and flush two hundred dollars

card.context: Talking about moderation in the last months of his life, Dick describes a habit his neighbour calls cognitive dissonance: he buys drugs and destroys them, scores marijuana and flushes two hundred dollars of it, because he enjoys scoring but does not want to. There are two ways not to be alive, he says — all the dope in the world, or all the hair shirts.
card.pith: Because I enjoy the feel of scoring but I don’t want to score.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: Drug misuse is not a disease, it is a decision

card.context: The note that ends the novel, in Dick's own voice. It is about people who were punished entirely too much for wanting a good time, like children playing in the street; the man Jerry Fabin is based on killed himself while it was being written. Drug misuse, he says, is a decision, and when many people make it, a life-style — only a speeding-up of ordinary life. There is no moral; there is Nemesis.
card.pith: Drug misuse is not a disease, it is a decision, like the decision to step out in front of a moving car.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: I myself, I am not a character in this novel; I am the novel.

card.context: The note continues: for a while Dick was himself one of the children playing in the street, and was punished; he is on the list of the dedicated, with what became of each. He is not a character, he says, but the novel — and so was the whole nation at that time.
card.pith: I myself, I am not a character in this novel; I am the novel.
card.speaker: Philip K. Dick

evidence.anchor: Once a guy stood all day shaking bugs from his hair

card.context: The novel's first sentence. Jerry Fabin, a burned-out user, spends eight hours in the shower trying to wash away aphids no one else can see, and works out their life cycle from the Britannica. Dick's Author's Note says the man Fabin is based on killed himself; Anne R. Dick's informants describe a housemate who did the same.
card.pith: Once a guy stood all day shaking bugs from his hair.
card.speaker: The narrator

evidence.anchor: is for Substance D. Which is for Dumbness and Despair and Desertion

card.context: Fred, the undercover agent in his scramble suit, gives a canned anti-drug talk to a Lions Club and goes off script. D is for dumbness, despair and desertion — and finally for death: Slow Death, "we, the dopers", call it. He has given himself away; his superior tells him he blew it.
card.pith: is finally Death. Slow Death
card.speaker: Fred (Bob Arctor)

evidence.anchor: The two hemispheres of my brain are competing?

card.context: The police psychologists give Fred his results: not simple impairment but competition between the hemispheres, two signals carrying conflicting information, because Substance D has damaged the dominant left side. The novel's split between Fred and Arctor is given a neurology — the same split-brain research Dick was reading in 1973–74.
card.pith: Substance D. It often causes that, functionally.
card.speaker: A police psychologist

evidence.anchor: I saw Substance D growing

card.context: The ending. Bruce, all that is left of Fred and Arctor, works on a New-Path farm and kneels before a field of small blue flowers hidden among corn: Mors ontologica, the source of Substance D, grown by the rehabilitation centre itself. He hides one in his shoe as a present for his friends.
card.pith: I saw death rising from the earth, from the ground itself, in one blue field, in stubbled color.
card.speaker: Bruce

evidence.anchor: It is addictive. From even one exposure

card.context: Kathy Sweetscent has tried JJ-180 once at a party in Tijuana. Next morning an agent of Earth's allies, the 'Starmen, tells her she is addicted after a single dose, that no clinic can cure it, and that they will supply her if she spies for them. She has taken dozens of drugs and never this. The drug is a weapon of a war.
card.pith: Of course it's addictive, Kathy; that's why we put you on it.
card.speaker: Corning

evidence.anchor: had a reputation for essaying an experience with every hallucinogenic drug

card.context: At the Tijuana party where JJ-180 is passed round, the guests include Marm Hastings, a wealthy author on oriental mysticism who tries every new hallucinogen and is examining his host's library on drugs and religion. He will ask, sharply, whether the drug is really German. Dick's satire of the religious drug-seeker, written around 1963–64.
card.pith: To Hastings this was allied with religion.
card.speaker: The narrator

evidence.anchor: He never did sleeping pills. He did uppers.

card.context: VALIS opens with a phone call: Gloria asks Horselover Fat for Nembutals so she can kill herself. His psychiatrist had told him to get off dope, which he hadn't done. He has no sleeping pills; he does uppers. He lies that he has ten, to keep her on the line. The narrator, who is also Fat, is telling the story of 1971.
card.pith: He never did sleeping pills. He did uppers.
card.speaker: The narrator (Horselover Fat)

evidence.anchor: It was like a plague. No one could discern how much was due to drugs.

card.context: After Gloria's suicide, Fat cries, watches TV and takes more dope; his own brain is going. Earlier the narrator has thanked Tim Leary for his promotion of expanded consciousness, and blamed Gloria's acid for wrecking her mind. Now the verdict on the whole Bay Area of the 1960s: it was like a plague, and no one could tell how much was drugs.
card.pith: It was like a plague. No one could discern how much was due to drugs.
card.speaker: The narrator (Horselover Fat)

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: The extent to which Phil used amphetamines while in Berkeley

card.context: Sutin on the 1950s. Doctors routinely prescribed amphetamine analogues such as Semoxydrine for anxiety and depression, and how much Dick used in Berkeley is "just isn't clear". A friend, Iskandar Guy, recalls regular low doses and a sophisticated knowledge of pharmacy; Dick's wife Kleo insists he took nothing but one sample from her father, a muscle relaxant and aspirin.
card.pith: But Kleo insists that, other than the Semoxydrine sample from her father, Phil took no drugs but Serpasil
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: By now it was a steady fuel for the writing

card.context: Sutin on the Point Reyes marriage, around 1960: Dick is hospitalised with chest pain diagnosed as pyloric spasm and told to cut down on coffee. Sutin asks whether the Semoxydrine came up, and answers that by then it was a steady fuel for the writing.
card.pith: By now it was a steady fuel for the writing.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: Newkom says that he gave Phil his first hit of acid sometime in 1964

card.context: Sutin dates Dick's first LSD to 1964, from Jack Newkom, and counts "at least two occasions" that year, one with Ray Nelson, who watched him relive a Roman gladiator's death in Latin. Phil never much liked it. Sutin quotes the July 1974 letter in which Dick says A Maze of Death depicts his 1964 LSD vision "with exact accuracy".
card.pith: He took it only a very few times, despite wild rumors that he often wrote on acid-rumors Phil resented but himself helped get started.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: What drugs these were is unknown

card.context: On the 1963 vision of the face in the sky. Sutin notes that Dick at the time described taking "certain chemicals" and "psychedelic drugs", that a 1967 letter rules out LSD, and that by the 1970s his accounts dropped the drugs altogether. His own view: amphetamines alone could do it — though anguish, not chemistry, was at the vision's heart.
card.pith: amphetamines alone, in sufficiently high doses, could account for such a vision
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: Acid, pot, and hash held no special fascination. But pills

card.context: Sutin on the marriage to Nancy Hackett, 1966–70. Drugs carried glamour in the sixties, and Timothy Leary made a fan call in 1969, but Dick's passion was pills: Stelazine, relaxants, Librium, Valium, Dexamyl and white crosses, prescription quality preferred. Nancy: "like he was medicating himself". His supply came from doctors to whom he recited the symptoms.
card.pith: Acid, pot, and hash held no special fascination. But pills … ah, pills.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: Ellison recalls that Phil assured him that both
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Sutin weighs the Dangerous Visions dispute. Ellison's 1967 introduction said "Faith of Our Fathers" and Palmer Eldritch came from hallucinogenic journeys; Ellison recalls that Dick assured him so, and Dick made no changes to the galleys. From 1975 the anthology carried Dick's rebuttal. Sutin believes the denial.
card.pith: It seems likely that Phil’s 1975 denial is truthful and that the 1967 version sounded fun at the time.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: said he was taking one thousand Methedrine tabs per week

card.context: From notes kept by Dick's stepfather in spring 1971: Phil phones to say he is a drug addict, "on Benzedrine and other drugs since 1951, when Kleo's physician father gave him a prescription". A girlfriend takes him to the psychiatric ward at Stanford, where the examining psychiatrist records a thousand Methedrine tablets a week at $300 a month, with Stelazine — and finds an "astute" intellect and no physical addiction.
card.pith: Phil said he was taking one thousand Methedrine tabs per week
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: bouts of intense paranoia are a known common side effect of amphetamine abuse

card.context: Santa Venetia, 1970–71: armed, unstable casualties of the drug scene in the house daily, a reasonable fear of rip-offs and busts — and jars of a thousand white crosses in the refrigerator next to protein milkshakes. Sutin will not choose between the real dangers and the drug: both are true.
card.pith: bouts of intense paranoia are a known common side effect of amphetamine abuse
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: X-Kalay stay lasted only three weeks

card.context: Sutin on X-Kalay: residents remembered as aged by decades, attack therapy that probed Dick's attraction to dark-haired girls — and a stay of only three weeks, after which its demands grated. Dick had told Vertex he pretended to be a heroin addict to get in; heroin, Sutin says, was one drug Dick never touched.
card.pith: X-Kalay stay lasted only three weeks
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: Never again did Phil take speed on a regular basis

card.context: Sutin's verdict on X-Kalay, which closed in 1976: whatever its faults, and Synanon's, it made Dick see the deadly folly of his amphetamine use. He never again took speed regularly.
card.pith: Never again did Phil take speed on a regular basis-this after nearly twenty years of steadily increasing doses.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: Phil accidentally took seven more grams of vitamin C than called for

card.context: Sutin traces the vitamin "recipe" to an article by the psychiatrist Harvey Ross, "Orthomolecular Psychiatry: Vitamin Pills for Schizophrenics", in Psychology Today for April 1974, and lists its doses of niacin, C, B6, B2 and E. Dick, he writes, took seven grams more vitamin C than called for — and never settled on a single cause.
card.pith: Phil accidentally took seven more grams of vitamin C than called for.
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: the only time he resorted to amphetamines in his final decade

card.context: September 1977: nervous about travelling to the Metz science fiction festival in France, where he was guest of honour, Dick scored a supply of speed. Sutin calls it the only time in his last decade.
card.pith: the only time he resorted to amphetamines in his final decade
card.speaker: Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Lawrence Sutin, Divine Invasions: A Life of Philip K. Dick (1989)

evidence.anchor: smoking some marijuana that a visitor had left

card.context: Tim Powers's account of March 1979, quoted by Sutin. Dick had smoked marijuana a visitor left behind, felt the familiar visionary state come on — "generally not dope-related — unless you count Vitamin C as dope" — and demanded to see God. He was flattened by terror and saw the Ark of the Covenant.
card.pith: he saw the Ark of the Covenant
card.speaker: Tim Powers, quoted by Lawrence Sutin

source.citation: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995; Tachyon edition 2010)

evidence.anchor: Phil took two Semoxydrine pills a day

card.context: Anne R. Dick on Phil moving into her Point Reyes house in 1958: he arrived with a closet-full of pills and medicines and loved to dose the girls' colds. She, raised a Christian Scientist, kept nothing in her medicine cabinet. He took two Semoxydrine a day, "prescribed for me years ago"; she did not ask what for.
card.pith: He didn’t tell me what for and I wasn’t interested enough to ask.
card.speaker: Anne R. Dick

source.citation: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995; Tachyon edition 2010)

evidence.anchor: Ray told me that there were a lot of illicit amphetamines around

card.context: Anne R. Dick on 1964, after Phil left Point Reyes for Oakland: Ray Nelson told her there were illicit amphetamines and rumours of dealing around the cottage Phil shared with Jack Newkom, and that Phil knew more about drugs than a pharmacist they knew. On her account, recreational use begins here — after the marriage.
card.pith: Phil started taking amphetamines “recreationally” at this time.
card.speaker: Anne R. Dick

source.citation: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995; Tachyon edition 2010)

evidence.anchor: He based his ideas on his reading about hallucinogenic mushrooms
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Anne R. Dick reads Palmer Eldritch against Phil's churchgoing in 1963–64: the novel sets the wafer of worldly pleasure, Can-D, against a spiritual wafer, Chew-Z, brought from the skies and made from a fungus. Phil did not know about LSD then, she says; his ideas came from reading about hallucinogenic mushrooms.
card.pith: Phil didn’t know about LSD at this time. He based his ideas on his reading about hallucinogenic mushrooms.
card.speaker: Anne R. Dick

source.citation: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995; Tachyon edition 2010)

evidence.anchor: He had such a bad trip that he never tried LSD again

card.context: Anne R. Dick's version of the LSD trip with Ray Nelson: eight hours of sweating, isolation, a spear thrust through the body, Latin, a Roman gladiator's life. On her account it was the only one.
card.pith: He had such a bad trip that he never tried LSD again.
card.speaker: Anne R. Dick

source.citation: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995; Tachyon edition 2010)

evidence.anchor: He took seventy pills a day

card.context: Anne R. Dick's informants on the late 1960s: Alys Graveson remembers Dexedrine, Benzedrine and antidepressants from three doctors, one later convicted for supplying addicts; Nancy Hackett gives the list — Stelazine, relaxants, Valium, tranquilisers, stimulants — and a number. Contaminated street speed then gave Phil acute pancreatitis.
card.pith: He took seventy pills a day.
card.speaker: Nancy Hackett, quoted by Anne R. Dick

source.citation: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995; Tachyon edition 2010)

evidence.anchor: He liked how he felt on speed

card.context: Cindy, a seventeen-year-old who came to the Santa Venetia house in 1970 with her boyfriend, Phil's methedrine supplier, told Anne R. Dick that Phil took a thousand "beans" a week, wrote, crashed for a week, and once flushed a thousand when a police car passed. He liked feeling powerful on speed. He would not touch pot.
card.pith: Phil wouldn’t touch pot, he hated it.
card.speaker: Cindy, quoted by Anne R. Dick

source.citation: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995; Tachyon edition 2010)

evidence.anchor: Although Phil kept telling Dr. A he was a drug addict

card.context: Late 1971: Dick asks his psychiatrist to hospitalise him for protection, and is admitted to the Marin mental health clinic. He keeps telling the doctor he is an addict; the doctor, seeing no withdrawal symptoms, thinks him a hypochondriac. Cindy, told this later: "Phil carried his 'beans' with him wherever he went."
card.pith: Dr. A believed Phil was just being hypochondriacal.
card.speaker: Anne R. Dick

source.citation: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick (1995; Tachyon edition 2010)

evidence.anchor: Doris believed he was off all drugs

card.context: Dick's last years in Santa Ana, as his friend Doris Sauter described them to Anne R. Dick: a quiet life, Thursday drinks at Tim Powers's, and no amphetamines at all. "He did a little grass, a little coke; that was all."
card.pith: He did a little grass, a little coke; that was all.
card.speaker: Doris Sauter, quoted by Anne R. Dick

source.citation: Kyle Arnold, The Divine Madness of Philip K. Dick (2016)

evidence.anchor: many have focused on the wrong drug: LSD

card.context: Arnold, a clinical psychologist, states his thesis in the introduction: Dick's paranoid episodes — the government agents, the 1971 hospitalisation — are "most parsimoniously explained" as byproducts of speed, which he had taken since childhood asthma. Commentators who blamed drugs picked the wrong one. Dick took LSD only occasionally.
card.pith: many have focused on the wrong drug: LSD
card.speaker: Kyle Arnold

source.citation: Kyle Arnold, The Divine Madness of Philip K. Dick (2016)

evidence.anchor: By age six, Dick was taking an amphetamine medication for asthma
evidence.editorial_note: Ephedrine is a related sympathomimetic stimulant, not an amphetamine in the strict pharmacological sense; both biographers call it one.

card.context: Arnold on Dick's childhood: separations, anxiety, difficulty swallowing, asthma — and ephedrine for the asthma by age six, "the first of many prescription drugs Dick was to use and abuse", starting the trajectory that ended in paranoid delusions. Sutin also mentions the asthma pill and calls it an amphetamine.
card.pith: By age six, Dick was taking an amphetamine medication for asthma called ephedrine.
card.speaker: Kyle Arnold

source.citation: Kyle Arnold, The Divine Madness of Philip K. Dick (2016)

evidence.anchor: he secretly wolfed down increasingly massive doses

card.context: Arnold reads the Point Reyes marriage clinically. Anne's memoir says the fights came from "no identifiable source"; Arnold adds Dick's past, and his amphetamines, taken in secret and in growing doses, with the paranoia that follows — the gate scene where Dick fled, believing Anne meant to run him over.
card.pith: During his marriage to Anne, he secretly wolfed down increasingly massive doses to fuel the frenetic pace of his writing.
card.speaker: Kyle Arnold

source.citation: Kyle Arnold, The Divine Madness of Philip K. Dick (2016)

evidence.anchor: All the symptoms some Dick scholars cite as evidence of schizophrenia

card.context: Against the diagnosis of schizophrenia, Arnold argues that Dick's paranoia around 1974 was not an onset but a chronic baseline built over years of amphetamine dependence, and that a writer of forty-four novels does not fit the typical picture of schizophrenia.
card.pith: All the symptoms some Dick scholars cite as evidence of schizophrenia can be explained by the amphetamine psychosis we know, beyond a shadow of a doubt, Dick had.
card.speaker: Kyle Arnold

source.citation: Kyle Arnold, The Divine Madness of Philip K. Dick (2016)

evidence.anchor: Some assert that he was still abusing amphetamines

card.context: Arnold on the medicines around February 1974: Percodan after the dental surgery, a diuretic for blood pressure, psychiatric drugs that may have included lithium. Some sources, he says, assert Dick was still abusing amphetamines; his wife Tessa did not see it, but he had hidden it from Anne too.
card.pith: Some assert that he was still abusing amphetamines.
card.speaker: Kyle Arnold

source.citation: Gregg Rickman, Philip K. Dick: In His Own Words (1984)

evidence.anchor: The facts appear to be that he was a heavy user of amphetamines for twenty years

card.context: Rickman's introduction, written two years after Dick's death, sets out to correct "more nonsense" than on any other subject: twenty years of heavy amphetamine use, from the early fifties to about 1973, legally over-prescribed; LSD only two or three times, and late. The collapsing realities of the novels, he concludes, come from imagination, not drugs.
card.pith: he took LSD only two or three times, and not ’til about 1967
card.speaker: Gregg Rickman

source.citation: Andrew M. Butler, Philip K. Dick (Pocket Essentials, revised edition)

evidence.anchor: with whom female colonists empathise on taking the illegal drug Can-D
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Butler's synopsis of Palmer Eldritch, whose text is not in this archive. Martian colonists take the illegal Can-D to inhabit the miniature world of Perky Pat; Eldritch returns from the Prox system with Chew-Z, which will make it obsolete. Butler lists the novel's ideas as bitheism, God as a real presence, transubstantiation.
card.pith: Explorer Palmer Eldritch has returned from the Prox System with a new drug, Chew-Z, which will make CanD obsolete.
card.speaker: Andrew M. Butler

source.citation: Fredric Jameson, Archaeologies of the Future (2005)

evidence.anchor: And this is precisely the case with Chew-Z
concepts: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch

card.context: Jameson on Dick's reversals. Where a reader assumes reality is being degraded, it turns out to be the dream-world that is degraded, infected by reality — and this is the case with Chew-Z, Palmer Eldritch's campaign to drive out the Perky Pat and Can-D monopoly.
card.pith: it turns out on the contrary that it is the dreamworld or hallucinatory state which is degraded, and progressively infected by reality itself
card.speaker: Fredric Jameson
